source: Nori et al. (2025) Sequential Diagnosis with Language Models: five MAI-DxO variants
finding: The paper defines variants (Instant Answer, Question Only, Budgeted, Unconstrained Budget, Ensemble) that change information access, budget or number of panels. It does not remove single roles such as Challenger or Hypothesis.
numbers: Five variants listed; o3 used for all MAI-DxO configurations; 304 NEJM cases, 56-case test set for the human comparison.
limits: Variants differ in several things at once, so no single role effect can be read off. Gap 2 stays open.
agent_relevance: Do not credit the challenger role alone. Test roles one at a time at equal cost in our own harness.

source: Nori et al. (2025) Sequential Diagnosis with Language Models: accuracy and cost per variant
finding: Unconstrained MAI-DxO with o3 beat off-the-shelf o3 on accuracy and cost. Budgeting cut cost with growing accuracy loss. Ensembling gave the top accuracy at about the cost of plain o3.
numbers: o3 78.6% at $7,850; MAI-DxO no budget 81.9% at $4,735; budgeted config 79.9% at $2,396; ensemble 85.5% at $7,184.
quote: MAI-DxO ... establishes a new Pareto frontier that outperforms off-the-shelf models and physicians at every cost or accuracy level.
limits: Ensemble is several independent runs plus aggregation, so part of its gain may be sampling, not role design. Costs are test costs, not tokens (inference about $0.15 per case).
agent_relevance: A budget gate trades accuracy for cost smoothly. Ensemble plus aggregation is a separable operator from role-play.

source: Nori et al. (2025) Sequential Diagnosis with Language Models: single versus batched mode ablation
finding: The only ablation reported on MAI-DxO (o3) compares single-step versus batched questions and tests. Accuracy was identical and single mode was cheaper.
numbers: Both 83.9% accuracy on the test set; cost $3,991 single versus $5,084 batched.
limits: Test set only (56 cases). Not a role ablation. Authors report the batched setting for realism.
agent_relevance: Asking for fewer tests per turn did not cost accuracy here. Small support for narrow, sequential evidence requests.

source: Nori et al. (2025) Sequential Diagnosis with Language Models: significance tests and model generality
finding: MAI-DxO gains were tested with a one-sided paired permutation test (10,000 resamples). Gains were larger for weaker models.
numbers: No-budget MAI-DxO gains significant for all models (p < 0.005) except o3 and o4-mini, which instead had significant cost reductions (p < 0.005); ensemble o3 accuracy gain p < 0.005.
quote: structured reasoning approach proved remarkably model-agnostic
limits: One benchmark; a model plays the gatekeeper (physicians reviewed 508 gatekeeper responses). Authors only hypothesize why it works.
agent_relevance: Structure helps weak models most. For a strong base model expect cost savings more than accuracy.

source: Nori et al. (2025) Sequential Diagnosis with Language Models: physician baseline details
finding: Physicians worked case by case with a UI and were far below the models.
numbers: 764 diagnoses over 56 cases, avg 36 cases per physician; 11.8 min per case; 6.6 questions, 7.2 tests; $2,963; accuracy 19.9%; best physician 41%.
limits: Generalists on hard NEJM cases in a restricted setting, so not a fair expert comparison.
agent_relevance: Human baselines in AI diagnosis papers are often generalists under artificial limits. Do not quote them as expert troubleshooting.

source: Pei et al. (2025) Flow-of-Action: SOP Enhanced LLM-Based Multi-Agent System for Root Cause Analysis: overall results table
finding: A system that follows a written standard operating procedure (SOP flow), with an action set and side agents, beat ReAct, CoT, Reflexion, K8sGPT and HolmesGPT on its own test bed. Gap 8 partly answered: SOP use is measured, the history-plus-SOP combination is not.
numbers: 90 incidents on one Google Online Boutique deployment; 9 injected anomaly types via ChaosMesh. GPT-4-Turbo: Flow-of-Action 64.01 avg (LA 70.89, TA 57.12) vs ReAct 35.50 (47.67/23.33). GPT-3.5: Flow-of-Action 54.06 (54.22/53.89) vs ReAct 21.89; GPT-3.5 Reflexion 54.06 average in the extracted table.
limits: One system, one author-made dataset, 9 fault types, no unseen-family split. Table is partly garbled in text extraction. K8sGPT and HolmesGPT handle one fault type only (11.11).
agent_relevance: A procedure retrieved from a library can double accuracy of a plain ReAct loop on known fault types. Says nothing about new fault families.

source: Pei et al. (2025) Flow-of-Action: SOP Enhanced LLM-Based Multi-Agent System for Root Cause Analysis: ablation of SOP and agents
finding: Removing SOP knowledge collapsed accuracy. Removing the SOP flow hurt location accuracy but less type accuracy. Removing the action set or any helper agent lowered accuracy moderately.
numbers: GPT-3.5 base, avg accuracy: full 54.06; w/o SOP knowledge 15.39; w/o SOP flow 27.50; w/o action set 42.34; one agent removed 33.67; w/o ActionAgent 34.39; w/o ObAgent 35.00 (row labels partly lost in extraction).
limits: Step limit of 20 caps path length so APL differences are muted. Single backbone, 90 incidents.
agent_relevance: Strongest evidence in this gap set that a scaffold part (a written procedure) carries most of the gain at fixed backbone.

source: Pei et al. (2025) Flow-of-Action: SOP Enhanced LLM-Based Multi-Agent System for Root Cause Analysis: action set size and step cap
finding: Location and type accuracy were roughly flat when the action set size changed, because the needed tools stayed in the set under SOP rules. A 20-step limit was imposed.
numbers: Figure 7 on a subset; no exact values read from text.
limits: Subset of the data; effect read from a figure.
agent_relevance: Bounded option lists matter less than having the right procedure in them. No token-budget curve by difficulty (gap 9 stays open).

source: Cai et al. (2026) AIOps2025 and RCA100 benchmarks: reasoning-process scoring
finding: The benchmark scores localization, fault type and whether the reasoning trace hits labelled key evidence, because a correct answer can come from keyword luck. Most scoring is deterministic with no LLM judge.
numbers: Over 500 expert-labelled cases, 2 systems; RCA100 weights 0.40 entity, 0.30 type, 0.30 reasoning process; AIOps2025 weights 0.40 / 0.40 / 0.10 explainability / 0.10 efficiency; 6,093 competition teams.
quote: a correct answer may result from keyword matching rather than systematic, evidence-grounded reasoning
limits: Dataset and design paper; the text read gives no agent accuracy table and no human re-score of the grader. Gap 10 only partly addressed.
agent_relevance: Lets us score our agent on quoted-evidence use, not just final label. A metric, not a tested fix (gap 7).

source: Cai et al. (2026) AIOps2025 and RCA100 benchmarks: case structure and difficulty
finding: Cases need several data types. RCA100 ground truth has causal chains with numeric checkpoints, so the agent must match values, not only name a metric.
numbers: AIOps2025: 400 cases, service 195 / pod 123 / node 82; 250 of 400 (62.5%) need two modalities and 124 need all three. RCA100: 103 cases (91 three-step chains, 12 four-step), 661 checkpoints (about 6.42 per case), 99.5% with numeric comparator; top four of 28 cause types cover 44.7%.
limits: Three SRE experts labelled and a senior adjudicated; no inter-rater numbers read.
agent_relevance: Cross-checking several data types is the norm in these cases, which matches experts' recursive evidence checks.

source: Hu and Ash (2026) Chat Debugging: An Exploratory Study of Human-AI Collaboration to Debug Analog Circuits: sample and design
finding: This resolves the 'not opened' flag for Hu and Ash. It is a chat-log thematic study of students using public LLMs on buggy breadboard and PCB circuits in a timed exam, not a think-aloud study of experts and not a benchmark.
numbers: 17 chat logs (5 in Spring 2025, 12 in Fall 2025) from a course of about 60 and 40 students; 6 problem types (e.g. flipped diode, upside-down opamp, probe setting); 30-minute hands-on exam.
limits: Self-selected, no accuracy rate, no control group. Authors call 17 small and self-selected. Does not test expert order of work (gap 4 stays open).
agent_relevance: Hardware troubleshooting with LLMs has only qualitative evidence so far.

source: Hu and Ash (2026) Chat Debugging: An Exploratory Study of Human-AI Collaboration to Debug Analog Circuits: strengths and failures of LLM help
finding: LLMs often listed the true root cause among zero-shot suggestions, but misread images of wiring and sounded sure when wrong. Students with weak basics handed over thinking.
numbers: Images used in 2 of 5 (Spring) and 5 of 12 (Fall) logs; one case where ChatGPT said it was 99% confident about wrong op-amp pins.
limits: Counts are of logs, not successes. No scoring of root-cause hit rate.
agent_relevance: Physical-world faults need sensing the agent cannot do from one photo. Add a rule: confidence must be tied to evidence the agent can check.

source: Ash and Hu (2026) WIP: Chat-Debugging: Large Language Model as a Hardware Debugging Assistant
finding: A single fourth-year student's chat logs and interviews using GPT-4o on hardware and software debugging. Successful sessions kept several LLM root-cause options open and the student corrected the LLM.
numbers: N = 1 student; qualitative themes by constant comparative analysis by two researchers.
limits: Case study. No numbers on success.
agent_relevance: Human leads, LLM supplies hypotheses: consistent with a multiple-hypotheses operator.

source: Schaafstal, Schraagen and van Berlo (2000) Cognitive task analysis and innovation of training: structured troubleshooting (abstract pages re-fetched)
finding: Two repository pages (Twente, TNO) give the same abstract and nothing more. Trained technicians solved about twice as many malfunctions in less time; the method was taught in less time.
numbers: No N, times or rates in any text opened. Gap 3 unresolved.
limits: Abstract only; full Human Factors 42(1):75-86 text not accessible. No replication found (search budget exhausted).
agent_relevance: Cite only as 'about twice as many'. Do not turn it into a number.

source: Search note: electronics hardware LLM fault benchmark query on arXiv search (2026-11-10)
finding: A site search for LLM electronic hardware fault diagnosis benchmark returned no results; a Hu and Ash query returned only the two chat-debugging papers. Weak evidence of absence from one query.
numbers: 0 hits for one query; Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex and arXiv export APIs were rate-limited and the WebSearch budget was used up.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 stays open: no measured non-IT benchmark found.

source: Search note: gaps 1, 6, 7 not testable from literature found
finding: No paper found that tests a complexity-type triage (gap 1), a no-fault gate (gap 6) or enforced quote-before-interpret grounding (gap 7). Only metrics like Cai's evidence checkpoints exist.
limits: Search was limited; this means not found, not nonexistent.
agent_relevance: These three remain our own ablations to run.
